title: Why tall parents have slightly shorter children
audience: A curious learner with no background in statistics

source.title: Regression towards Mediocrity in Hereditary Stature
source.venue: Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 15, pp. 246–263

intro.summary: Galton compared the heights of 930 adult children with those of their 205 pairs of parents. Children of unusually tall or unusually short parents were, on average, less unusual than their parents: about two-thirds as far from the average. He called this “regression towards mediocrity”. Today it is called regression to the mean, and it shows up wherever two measurements are related but not perfectly.
background: An average (mean) is the typical value of a group.
A deviation is how far one value sits above or below the average. Galton called it a “deviate”.
Galton put women's heights on the men's scale by multiplying them by 1.08, so that all heights could be compared directly.
intro.aha: Tall parents have children who are tall, but less so than themselves, and the same pull towards the average appears whenever two measurements are only partly linked.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body:
In the 1880s nobody knew how traits pass from parents to children. Genes hadn't been discovered. Francis Galton, a Victorian scientist and Charles Darwin's cousin, wanted to find a rule for it that he could measure.

He picked height because it's easy to measure and everyone has some. If tall parents had tall children, by how much? And what happened to the children of very short parents?
primer.quote: My object is to place beyond doubt the existence of a simple and far-reaching law that governs the hereditary transmission of, I believe, every one of those simple qualities which all possess, though in unequal degrees.

primer.heading: A clue from seeds
primer.body:
Years earlier Galton had friends across Britain grow sweet peas from seeds of different sizes. The results puzzled him. The plants grown from very large seeds made seeds that were smaller than their parents. The plants grown from very small seeds made seeds that were larger. Either way, the next generation landed nearer the middle.

He wanted to know whether people worked the same way.
primer.quote: the offspring did not tend to resemble their parent seeds in size, but to be always more mediocre than they
primer.quote_where: Opening section, on the seed experiments

primer.heading: What he did
primer.body:
Galton offered prizes for detailed family records and got the heights of hundreds of families. Women are shorter than men on average, so he multiplied every woman's height by 1.08 to put everyone on the same scale.

For each family he summed the two parents up as one number, their average height, and compared it with how tall their grown-up children were. The first exhibit shows why one number per couple was enough.
primer.quote: My data consisted of the heights of 930 adult children and of their respective parentages, 205 in number.

primer.heading: What he found
primer.body:
Tall parents did have tall children, but on average the children were less tall than their parents. Short parents had short children, but less short. The children kept only about two-thirds of their parents' distance from the average height, whichever way it went.

Galton called this “regression towards mediocrity”, where mediocrity just meant the average. The second exhibit lets you measure the two-thirds yourself.

primer.heading: Why it matters
primer.body:
The same pattern turns up far beyond height. Pick out a group because it scored unusually high or low on one measurement, and on a second, partly linked measurement it will usually look less unusual. That's true of test scores, sports seasons and patients who start a treatment when they feel worst. Today it's called regression to the mean, and mistaking it for a real effect is one of the most common errors in reading data. The last exhibit shows where it comes from.

Galton's own explanation leaned on remote ancestors and came before genetics, so it doesn't hold up. The statistical pattern he found does. He also knew families might have recorded heights carelessly, and argued that honest errors couldn't produce such a consistent result.
primer.quote: I now can securely contemplate the possibility of the records of height having been frequently drawn up in a careless fashion

concepts.title: One number for two parents
concepts.idea: Galton summarised both parents by their average height, the mid-parent, and found that the gap between the parents hardly mattered.

predict.question: Couple A: a 75-inch father and a 59-inch mother. Couple B: a 67-inch father and a 64-inch mother. Going by Galton's finding, whose children would you expect to be taller, on average?
options: Couple B's: they're the better-matched pair
Couple A's, slightly: their mid-parent is higher
You can't say: a tall-and-short couple has children of every height
why: Being well matched doesn't add height. Only the average counts, and on the men's scale B's mid-parent is about 68 inches against A's 69⅓.
Right. Put each mother on the men's scale (× 1.08) and average: A comes to about 69⅓, B to about 68. The big gap between A's parents hardly matters.
Galton found that very different couples had children much like matched couples with the same average, so the mid-parent still tells you what to expect.

model.title: Two parents, one number
model.note: Teaching model: just Galton's arithmetic for the mid-parent. The heights are example values, not records from his data.

steps.say: Three bars: a father, a mother, and one number that stands for the pair, their average.
This slider sets the father's height. Watch his bar follow it.
This one sets the mother's. Galton multiplied women's heights by 1.08 to put everyone on the men's scale.
The boxes under the chart read out the numbers as anything moves.

explore.prompt: Play with the two parents and watch the average bar. Very different couples can share the same average.

goals.text: Make the mother exactly as tall as the father on the men's scale (within 0.3 in)
hints: Only the mother's slider changes her bar.
Her bar is her height times 1.08. You need that to reach the father's 70.
70 ÷ 1.08 is about 64.8, so try a mother of about 65 inches.

goals.text: Find a couple more than 8 inches apart whose average is the population average, 68¼ in (within 0.3 in)
hints: Pull the parents far apart first, then fix the average.
Make the father tall and the mother short, then nudge one until the average box reads about 68¼.
A father of about 73 with a mother of about 59 works.

feedback.correct: Right. Couple A's mid-parent is about 69⅓ inches and Couple B's about 68, and the gap between A's parents makes little difference.
feedback.incorrect: It's natural to think a mismatched couple is less predictable. Galton found the gap barely matters: only the mid-parent does, and Couple A's is higher.

understand.explanation: Galton grouped families by how different the two parents were and compared how spread out the children's heights were. The groups looked alike. So he could replace two parents with one number, the mid-parent, as the walkthrough showed. He noted one exception he couldn't confirm: daughters seemed to take slightly more after their fathers.
understand.quote: It is therefore certain that differences in the heights of the parents have on the whole an inconsiderable effect on the heights of their offspring.

steps.say: Start with a 70-inch father and a 62-inch mother. On the men's scale she counts as 67.
Galton called the average of those two bars the mid-parent: here 68½.
Now a very tall father with a very short mother…
…and an evenly matched couple. Their mid-parents are almost the same, and Galton found their children looked alike too.

connect.caption: Galton multiplied each mother's height by 1.08 to put it on the men's scale, then averaged it with the father's height. Each coloured term matches a slider or a number in the model.

concepts.recap: Galton replaced two parents with one number, their average or mid-parent, because the gap between them barely mattered.

terms.means: The average of the father's height and the mother's height on the men's scale (her height × 1.08).

concepts.title: Children are two-thirds as unusual
concepts.idea: On average, a child's deviation from the population average is about two-thirds of the mid-parent's deviation.

predict.question: Some mid-parents are 6 inches above average (74¼ in, taller than the model goes). With Galton's two-thirds rule, how tall would you expect their adult children to be, on average?
options: About 74¼ in: as tall as their parents
About 72¼ in: tall, but less so
why: Like parent, like child feels right, but children keep only about two-thirds of their parents' lead.
Right. Two-thirds of a 6-inch lead is 4 inches, and 68¼ + 4 = 72¼.
That would mean nothing is passed on. Tall parents' children are still tall, just less so.
Children taller than already-tall parents would push heights further apart each generation, which doesn't happen.

model.title: Expected child height for each mid-parent
model.note: Teaching model: a straight-line rule for the average child. Real children scatter widely around this line, and the 68¼-inch average is Galton's figure for his population.

controls.label: Share of the lead passed on

steps.say: Across: a mid-parent's height. Up: how tall their children turn out, on average.
The dashed diagonal means 'like parent, like child': children exactly as tall as their mid-parents.
This slider picks a mid-parent. The point slides along the line.
This one sets how much of the parents' lead over the average gets passed on. At zero, every child is expected at the average.

explore.prompt: Galton found that the children of 72-inch mid-parents averaged about 70¾ inches. Tilt the line to match his data, then try parents below average.

goals.text: Set the share passed on so that the children of 72-inch mid-parents average 70¾ in (within 0.15 in)
hints: Leave the mid-parent at 72 and move only the share passed on.
At 1 the children match the parents; at 0 they're average. You want somewhere in between.
A share of about 0.65 gets close to 70¾.

goals.text: Keeping a share near two-thirds, find mid-parents whose children average 1 inch below the average (67¼ in, within 0.1 in)
hints: Keep the share near two-thirds, then move the mid-parent below the average.
The child should end up 1 inch below average, so the parents must be about 1½ inches below.
Try a mid-parent of about 66¾ inches.

feedback.correct: Yes. Two-thirds of the 6-inch lead is kept: about 4 inches above average, or 72¼ inches.
feedback.incorrect: Most people expect children to match their parents. On average they don't: they keep about two-thirds of the lead, so 6 inches becomes about 4.

understand.explanation: The solid line is flatter than the diagonal, so on average a child is less unusual than its mid-parent, in either direction. Children of tall parents are still tall, just less so, and children of short parents are short, but less so. This is an average: individual children scatter well above and below the line. That scatter is why the population doesn't get less varied with each generation.
understand.quote: the height-deviate of the offspring is, on the average, two-thirds of the height-deviate of its mid-parentage.

steps.say: If children inherited the whole lead, 72-inch mid-parents would have 72-inch children.
If they inherited none of it, their children would be plain average: 68¼.
Galton measured about two-thirds of the deviate passed on: those children average about 70¾. Tall, but less so.
Below the average it works the same way: children of short parents are pulled up towards the middle.

connect.caption: Galton's law of regression: the child's deviate is, on average, two-thirds of the mid-parent's deviate. The ⅔ is the share you set with the slider.

concepts.recap: On average, children keep about two-thirds of their mid-parents' distance from the average height.

terms.means: Galton's word for how far a height sits above or below the average.

concepts.title: Where the regression comes from
concepts.idea: When two measurements are only partly linked, people picked for an extreme first measurement are, on average, less extreme on the second.

predict.question: A school gives extra coaching to the 10% of pupils with the lowest marks. On the next test, that group scores much closer to the average. What does this tell you about the coaching?
options: It worked: the group clearly improved
Not much on its own: a group picked for low marks would move towards the average anyway
It backfired: the group should have improved even more
why: The group did score better, but some of their low first marks were bad luck that won't repeat. They'd have moved up even with no coaching.

Right. Two tests are only partly linked, so a group picked for extreme first marks drifts towards the average on the second. To judge the coaching you'd compare with similar pupils who weren't coached.
Nothing here says what the group 'should' have scored. The pull towards the average happens by itself, so you need an uncoached group to compare with.

model.title: Picking extremes from paired measurements
model.note: Teaching model: simulated pairs of measurements with a chosen correlation, in standard-deviation units. They illustrate the mechanism and are not Galton's records.

controls.label: How strongly the two measurements are linked (r)

explore.prompt: Each dot is a person: first measurement across, second measurement up. The highlighted dots are the ones picked for a high first measurement. Weaken the link and watch where they land on the second.

goals.text: Make the selected group keep about two-thirds of its extremeness, like Galton's children (within 3 points of 67%)
hints: Only the link changes how much is kept.
A tight link keeps almost everything; no link keeps nothing. Aim for the middle.
A link of about 0.65 keeps about two-thirds.

goals.text: Make the second measurement tell you nothing about the first, so the extremeness all but vanishes (under 5%)
hints: What happens as the link gets weaker?
Push the link all the way down.

feedback.correct: Right. Picking the lowest scorers guarantees some rise on the next test, coaching or not. You'd need a comparison group to see what the coaching added.
feedback.incorrect: It looks like the coaching worked, but a group picked for an extreme first score moves towards the average on a second, partly linked score anyway. That's regression to the mean, and it fools people all the time.

understand.explanation: Anyone picked for an extreme first value got there partly through what the two measurements share and partly through luck that isn't shared. On the second measurement, the shared part carries over and the luck doesn't. So the group keeps about r of its lead, whichever share you select. Galton explained it with ancestry: a child inherits partly from the parents and partly from a long line of ancestors whose average is the population average, like water poured into wine. Modern genetics tells the story differently, but the statistical pattern he found holds.
understand.quote: The child inherits partly from his parents, partly from his ancestry.

steps.say: With a tight link, the picked group stays almost as far ahead on the second measurement.
Loosen the link. Part of what put these people at the top was luck, and luck doesn't repeat.
With no link at all, the group lands right back on the average.
Galton's heights sit about here: roughly two-thirds kept. This pull back towards the average is called regression to the mean.

check.task: Select the top half instead of the top 10%, and set the link so the group again keeps about two-thirds of its extremeness (within 4 points of 67%).
check.hint: The share kept depends on how strongly the measurements are linked, not on how extreme the selected group is.
check.misconception: It is easy to think regression only affects the most extreme cases. Any group selected on the first measurement keeps about r of its lead.

connect.caption: When both measurements have the same spread, the share of the deviation that carries over equals the correlation r. Galton's two-thirds plays the role of r for mid-parents and their children.

concepts.recap: Regression to the mean happens whenever two measurements are only partly linked: an extreme first value is partly luck that doesn't repeat.

steps.say: Each dot is a person measured twice: the first measurement across, the second up.
The highlighted dots are the people picked for a high first measurement. This slider sets what share gets picked.
This one sets how strongly the two measurements are linked. Near 1 they almost always agree.
The boxes track the picked group: where it sits on each measurement, and how much of its lead it keeps.

terms.means: An extreme group looking less extreme on a second, partly linked measurement.
